lines.text: Trang-keh-bar, southern India, sixteen sixty.
The king of Tan-jore's army has surrounded the town,
and it will stay for nine months.
Inside the walls, the man in charge can barely read.
He has no orders, no money and no ships from home.
Denmark has forgotten him.
So why is he still flying its flag?
His name was Es-kil An-der-sen,
called Kongs-bak-keh after his hometown,
then part of Denmark and now in Sweden.
He was a commoner, nobody important.
But he was stubborn, and that would matter.
In sixteen thirty-nine he joined the Danish East India Company
and sailed for its only fort in India,
Dans-borg, at Trang-keh-bar.
The Danes rented the village from the Naa-yuk of Tan-jore,
in return for a yearly tribute.
But the voyage was so hard
that his ship, the Kris-chans-hown,
only reached India in sixteen forty-three.
Nobody aboard knew it yet,
but it would be the last Danish ship to arrive
for twenty-six years.
But soon the colony began to fall apart.
In sixteen forty-eight, the garrison mutinied
and arrested its own governor.
Back home, Denmark was worn down by wars with Sweden,
so no ships could be spared.
Therefore, in sixteen fifty,
the bankrupt company was simply dissolved.
Trang-keh-bar was now an orphan:
a fort, a few soldiers,
and a rent bill nobody in Copenhagen meant to pay.
Kongs-bak-keh, now the fort's quartermaster,
did the one thing he could.
He made the soldiers stand guard and drill,
as if help were coming.
On the seventh of September, sixteen fifty-five,
the governor, Pole Han-sen Kor-sur, died.
No Danish officer was left to replace him.
So the soldiers and townspeople
chose the quartermaster.
An almost illiterate commoner
was now in charge of Denmark's only colony in India.
And almost at once, he had an enemy.
The Naa-yuk of Tan-jore, Vi-jaya Raa-gha-va,
needed money for his own wars against Jin-jee and Ma-doo-rai.
He saw a weak colony,
and he raised the rent.
Kongs-bak-keh could not pay,
so the Naa-yuk sent an army.
But Kongs-bak-keh had planned for this.
With Portuguese mercenaries and local Indian allies,
he held the fort, and the siege was lifted.
He knew the Naa-yuk would be back.
So he started building.
Until then, only the fort was defended.
When danger came, the townspeople crowded inside.
So Kongs-bak-keh had a wall built around the whole town,
with new towers for cannon.
Historians still argue over how much of that wall was really his.
But when the Naa-yuk returned in sixteen sixty,
the siege lasted nine months,
and Trang-keh-bar still did not fall.
Holding a wall, though, costs money.
And he had none.
So the commander became a trader,
and sometimes a privateer.
He sent cargoes east to Ban-tam in Java,
and to Ma-kas-sar.
He waged a private war at sea
against the Mughal governor of Bengal,
seized his ships and sold their cargo.
The profits paid for soldiers and for repairs to Dans-borg.
He sent hopeful reports home to Copenhagen.
Copenhagen did not believe them.
By sixteen sixty-eight, even Kongs-bak-keh thought
the colony could not survive alone.
So he sent one last messenger,
a Dutchman named Hairt van Haa-gen,
all the way to Copenhagen.
This time, it worked.
In May sixteen sixty-nine,
a Danish frigate, the Fair-uh,
dropped anchor off Trang-keh-bar.
One of its officers, Hen-rik Eg-gers,
carried instructions for what to do
if Kongs-bak-keh was dead and the town was lost.
Instead, he found Kongs-bak-keh alive,
and the colony in good order.
Peace with the Naa-yuk soon followed,
and it even gave the Danes new villages.
You might expect a hero's welcome.
He got the opposite.
Eg-gers and his officers looked down
on the commoner who could barely write,
and pushed him aside.
Kongs-bak-keh complained bitterly:
that is the honour one gets
for five years of service in Europe,
and thirty years in India.
The king backed him, and called Eg-gers home.
Kongs-bak-keh stayed in command at Dans-borg
until he died, around sixteen seventy-four.
He never saw home again.
For a long time, Danish historians called him
the loyal man who saved the colony.
Today, some argue the story is less simple.
Trang-keh-bar was a multicultural town,
he may have married an Indian woman,
and trading inside Asia may have paid better
than waiting for ships from Copenhagen.
Maybe that is the real lesson.
Kongs-bak-keh did not survive because Denmark helped him.
He survived because he stopped waiting for Denmark,
and became part of India.
And because he held on,
the Danish flag flew over Trang-keh-bar
for another hundred and seventy years.
